A note on evidence

Hauntings and supernatural powers are not established by the sources here. We separate documented history, literary or oral tradition, paranormal claims, and criminal allegations. A real crime described as “occult” is evidence of a reported crime—not proof that a spell or spirit exists. Present-day allegations are summarized without graphic detail; accused people are not described as convicted unless the linked source says so.

The 2001 Monkey Man scare—on record

AP ARCHIVE · DELHI · MAY 2001

What the footage records

The archive description identifies Delhi footage from 15–16 May 2001, including residents, police, and newspaper headlines about the rumour.

Evidence boundary: the footage supports that the rumour, reporting, and public fear occurred. It does not establish that an unknown or supernatural attacker existed.

Historical lens · c. 6th—13th century and beyond

Tantra was a tradition, not a horror genre.

“Tantra” covers diverse Hindu and Buddhist traditions built around sacred texts and practices. Some histories look uncanny from the outside; that does not make Tantra a synonym for black magic. Practices differed by lineage, place, period, teacher, and text.

At a high level, sources describe initiation and guidance, mantra, deity visualization, yoga, diagrams such as yantras or mandalas, and ritual offerings. Particular Shaiva and Shakta streams also used cremation-ground settings or taboo symbolism. These were specialized traditions—not a universal checklist, and not evidence that supernatural claims are true.

Respectful boundary: this is historical context, not a how-to. The archive does not publish ritual recipes, instructions involving human remains, or advice to trespass or harm anyone. A modern crime described as “tantrik” does not represent Tantra as a whole.
Read the British Museum overview ↗
c. 500–600 CE

Texts take shape

The British Museum dates Tantra's emergence in India to around the 6th century. There is no single founding text or single origin story.

By the 700s

Across traditions

Tantric texts were studied in Hindu and Buddhist settings; lineages exchanged ideas as the traditions developed.

c. 800–1300

Temples, images, and Yoginis

Patrons commissioned temples and powerful goddess imagery. Roofless Yogini temples and their sculptures are material heritage—not evidence of haunting.

In some lineages

Facing fear and taboo

Cremation-ground meditation, ash, or skull imagery appear in specific sources. The symbolism could confront mortality, disgust, and attachment; it was never “what all Tantrikas did.”

Sources: British Museum, What is Tantra? and A timeline of Tantra. These are broad museum summaries; specialist scholarship continues to debate origins and particular practices.

WORLD FILES / 01—03

These are not “proof” of a universal ghost. They are region-specific traditions with their own histories, storytellers, and meanings.

Compare motifs, not cultures: a voice in the night, a warning at a threshold, a figure beside a river. Similar fears can appear in different places without implying a shared cause or identical belief.
